title: UK government AI strategy not tied to US models that currently dominate
content:

UK government AI strategy not tied to US models that currently dominate
Cabinet Office says its central government AI strategy means it is not tied to the models suppliers use today
The UK government is ensuring it does not remain reliant on artificial intelligence (AI) models from US companies through its tool development.
Last week, a freedom of information (FOI) request response revealed that 10 out of 11 AI tools used in central government rely on AI models from US suppliers.
The response to questions from UK AI firm Aventail revealed that the government uses models from Google, OpenAI, Microsoft and Anthropic directly or through Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services (AWS). The only exception to US firms is PolyAI, a UK company whose models are used by the government’s shared services provider, SSCL.
Such reliance stokes fears of a lack of control over models, pricing or access changes, but the government has since told Computer Weekly that its development of tools ensures it is not tied to suppliers. Rather, it wants to benefit from the AI available today without locking itself into decisions that might limit its choices in the future.
Decoupled from suppliers
A government spokesperson said: “Government AI tools developed by teams like GDS [the Government Digital Service] and i.AI [the Incubator for Artificial Intelligence] are engineered around decoupled, model-agnostic architectures. By separating our data pipelines, user interfaces, and retrieval mechanisms from the underlying foundation models, we avoid hardcoding government applications into any single vendor’s ecosystem.”
The spokesperson added that commercially available models via secure enterprise agreements have allowed civil servants to safely prototype and deliver “immediate efficiency”.
“However, maintaining modular API [application programming interface] and orchestration layers ensures we retain the operational resilience to evaluate, swap, or self-host alternative models as capabilities mature,” they added.
Joe Ward, co-founder and CEO of UK AI company Aventail, who submitted the FOI questions that revealed the government’s heavy reliance on US AI models, said: “Model-agnostic design is the right approach and the government deserves credit for thinking about model flexibility.”
But he added: “The key test for the British government: if the US president revoked access to every US model overnight, would our AI systems stay afloat? Resilience depends on both adaptability and speed.”
In its FOI response, the Cabinet Office confirmed that Google Gemini is the primary authorised enterprise-level generative AI tool. Other AI tools used include Hansard AI for parliamentary and legislative research, Minute for creating meeting notes, and GCS Assist for government communications.
It also said it had a contingency plan but could not reveal details. “The information contains details about the detection and prevention of crime which would assist criminals to plan and execute criminal acts and to avoid detection. Disclosure would thus make the prevention of certain crimes more difficult and reduce the effectiveness of the police service in detecting the perpetrators,” it said in the response.
Technology agnostic, not dependent
During a speech last month, UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan emphasised the importance of Britain remaining technology agnostic.
“We want the world’s leading companies to invest here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment,” he said.
Framing the government’s policy on AI around what matters to UK citizens, he said technology infrastructure should not be built simply because a company wants it. “We must be clear about what Britain needs and what our people receive in return,” said Narayan. “British national interest will be and must be our guiding principle.”
He warned that the country does not control the technology it uses. “Much of the technology that will shape our economy, our public services, and our national security is being developed outside this country,” said Narayan.
The UK’s reliance on technology that isn’t home-grown is, for Narayan, a question of national security, as well as what he called “a question of democratic power”.
“If the British state cannot exercise meaningful control over the technologies on which our country depends, neither can the people that it represents,” he said.

report.summary: UK government says its AI tools use model-agnostic architectures to avoid lock-in to dominant US suppliers, despite an FOI revealing heavy reliance on American models.
report.background: Governments are racing to adopt generative AI, but central agencies often depend on a small group of US foundation-model providers such as OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic. A Freedom of Information request by UK AI firm Aventail found that 10 of 11 AI tools used in UK central government rely on US models, directly or through Microsoft Azure and AWS; the only UK exception is PolyAI, used by shared-services provider SSCL. The finding raised concerns about control over pricing, access, data handling and national security. The Cabinet Office says tools built by the Government Digital Service and i.AI use decoupled, model-agnostic architectures so applications are not hardcoded to one vendor. AI minister Kanishka Narayan has framed technology agnosticism as a national-interest issue: the UK wants investment from leading companies but rejects dependence as the price.
key_points: An FOI response obtained by Aventail shows that 10 of 11 AI tools in central government rely on US models from Google, OpenAI, Microsoft and Anthropic, directly or via Azure and AWS. PolyAI, a UK company used by SSCL, is the only exception.

The Cabinet Office says government AI tools are built around decoupled, model-agnostic architectures. Data pipelines, user interfaces and retrieval systems are separated from foundation models, while modular API and orchestration layers allow officials to evaluate, swap or self-host alternative models as capabilities mature.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan says the UK must remain technology agnostic but not dependent. He argues that control over technology is a national-security and democratic-power issue, warning that much of the technology shaping the economy and public services is developed outside the UK.

Google Gemini is the primary authorised enterprise-level generative AI tool. Other named tools include Hansard AI for parliamentary and legislative research, Minute for meeting notes, and GCS Assist for government communications. The Cabinet Office says it has a contingency plan but withheld details, citing crime-prevention risks.
report.impact: The UK’s stance signals that public-sector AI procurement may shift toward interoperability, multi-model orchestration and sovereign options rather than single-vendor deals. For the AI industry, it creates demand for model-agnostic platforms and UK or open-weight alternatives, while putting pressure on US providers to offer better terms and resilience guarantees. For developers, the lesson is to build abstraction layers, avoid hardcoding to one API, and design for rapid model switching or self-hosting. For regular users, the hope is continuity of public services if access or pricing changes, though swapping models can bring performance differences, retraining costs and slower feature rollouts. The bigger test is whether the UK can move from architectural flexibility to operational speed.
report.tools: For readers tracking model-agnostic AI, watch LiteLLM for open-source API routing, LangChain and LlamaIndex for orchestration, OpenRouter for multi-model access, and Ollama or vLLM for self-hosting open-weight models. Hugging Face remains useful for evaluating alternatives. Also follow GDS and i.AI engineering updates for public-sector patterns around decoupled architectures and model swapping.
